candidate_analysis.explanation: The Random Forest classified this binary as MALWARE with probability 1.0000, and all 20 top n-grams have positive SHAP contributions toward cryptojacking (+0.0069 to +0.0170). The n-grams form two coherent clusters typical of CPU-bound hashing/mining code. First, SSE2 vector and bit-mixing patterns: PXOR MOVAPS (+0.01704), PXOR PXOR (+0.01379), PXOR MOVDQA (+0.01332), MOVDQA PXOR (+0.00873), LEA MOVDQA (+0.00944), LEA PXOR (+0.00711), PADDQ MOVDQA (+0.00715), MOVQ PUNPCKLQDQ (+0.01013), MOVHLPS MOVQ (+0.01142), ADD MOVQ (+0.00946) and CALL MOVQ (+0.00865). These indicate heavy 128-bit XOR, move, add and lane-shuffle work, as in state-mixing steps of memory-hard hash functions. Second, rotate and integer-mix patterns: XOR ROL (+0.01090), MOV ROL (+0.00900), ROL ROR (+0.00887), ADD ROR (+0.00846), ROL ADD (+0.00725), ROL MOV (+0.00694), SHL OR (+0.00864), SUB ADC (+0.01014) and DIV MUL (+0.00773). These resemble ARX-style round functions and multi-precision arithmetic seen in hashing and cryptographic primitives. Because many of these n-grams occur at relatively high frequency (PXOR MOVDQA 0.001891, MOVQ PUNPCKLQDQ 0.006958, SHL OR 0.002329), they reflect sustained computation rather than incidental occurrences. The evidence gives no function names or API calls, so I cannot confirm mining-specific behavior such as pool communication. The combined signal of the model output and the consistent mix of vector XOR/shuffle and rotate/add patterns strongly supports a cryptojacking classification, though these instruction patterns also appear in legitimate crypto or compression code.

evidence_analysis.assessment: Strongest contributor. SSE XOR followed by an aligned 128-bit move suggests vectorized state mixing and storing, typical of hash scratchpad operations. The frequency is low, but the signal is highly discriminative.
Consecutive 128-bit XORs indicate dense vectorized mixing, consistent with the inner loops of mining hash algorithms.
Vector XOR paired with aligned 128-bit data movement is consistent with block-wise XOR of hash state. Its relatively high frequency (0.001891) suggests repeated use.
High-to-low lane shuffling followed by a 64-bit extract is typical when combining or reducing 128-bit state values in hash code.
XOR combined with rotation is a core ARX/hash round primitive and supports cryptographic or hashing computation.
Subtract followed by add-with-carry indicates multi-word arithmetic, used in big-integer math and some hash or PoW computations.
The most frequent top-20 n-gram (0.006958). Packing 64-bit values into 128-bit registers suggests sustained SIMD data preparation for hash rounds.
Integer addition combined with 64-bit XMM transfers suggests mixing scalar and vector computation, as in optimized hashing loops.
Address computation followed by an aligned 128-bit load or store suggests structured buffer or scratchpad access.
Loading a value and then rotating it is consistent with bit-diffusion steps in cryptographic or hash rounds.
Opposing rotations in sequence are characteristic of hash and cipher mixing functions.
The load-then-XOR ordering complements PXOR MOVDQA, indicating repeated vector XOR of memory blocks.
A call followed by a 64-bit XMM move suggests helper routines that return or handle vector or hash values. Without function context, this is weaker evidence.
Shift-and-combine is common for bit packing and for emulating rotates or assembling words in hashing. It also occurs in general code, so it is moderately specific.
Addition followed by rotation matches the ARX round structure used in many hash and cipher algorithms.
Very rare (0.000004) but pushes toward malware. It suggests big-number or modular arithmetic, though on its own it is ambiguous.
Rotate followed by add is another ARX pattern, reinforcing the hashing-primitive interpretation.
64-bit packed addition with aligned vector moves suggests SIMD arithmetic on hash state.
Address calculation followed by vector XOR suggests XOR against computed buffer offsets, consistent with scratchpad-style access.
Rotate followed by move continues the rotate-heavy pattern, supporting bit-mixing routines.
